content: The Annex A Guideline Steering Group includes a diverse range of professionals and experts in the field of sexual and reproductive health. Members such as Lynn Bakimajian, Carmen Barroso, Leo Bryant, Jane Cottingham, Nel Druce, Lynn Freedman, Sofia Gruskin, Karen Hardee, Jane Hobson, Sandra Jordan, Eszter Kismodi, Jan Kumar, Karen Newman, Mariela Rodriguez, and Kate Shaw have contributed to the development of these guidelines. Additionally, WHO staff members Maria Rodriguez, Monica Dragoman, Rajat Khosla, Lale Say, and Marleen Temmerman have also played a significant role in this effort. The Annex B Guideline Development Group emphasizes that the opinions expressed in the document are those of the individual contributors and do not necessarily reflect the policies or opinions of their associated organizations or countries. Members of this group include Alfonso Barrangues (UNFPA, USA), Harriet Birungi (Population Council, Kenya), Shelah S. Bloom (MEASURE Evaluation, University of North Carolina, USA), Dirk Van Braeckel (Ghent University, Belgium), Jacqueline Bryld (Danish Family Planning Association, Denmark), Caroline Phiri Chibwe (Ministry of Community Development, Zambia), Jacqueline Darroch (Guttmacher Institute, USA), Suzanne Ehlers (Population Action International, USA), Faustina Fynn-Nyame (Marie Stopes International, Ghana), Christine Galavotti (Sexual, Reproductive, and Maternal Health CARE, USA), Baochang Gu (Renmin University of China, China), Demet Güral (Pathfinder International, USA), Krishna Jafa (Population Services International, India), Sandra Jordan (USAID, USA), Jane Kiragu (Satima Consultants Ltd, Kenya), Sunita Kishor (MEASURE DHS, USA), Rebecca Koladycz (International Planned Parenthood Federation, USA), Tamara Kreinin (The David and Lucile Packard Foundation, USA), Matthew Lindley (International Planned Parenthood Federation, UK), Nyovani J. Madise (University of Southampton, UK), Tarek Meguid (University of Namibia, Namibia), Poonam Muttreja (Population Foundation of India, India), Nuriye Ortayli (Reproductive Health, UNFPA, USA), Jacqueline Pitanguy (CEPIA, Brazil), Melanie Plenert (Wits Reproductive Health and HIV Research Institute, South Africa), Serge Rabier (Equilibres & Populations, France), Scott Radloff (Bill & Melinda Gates Institute for Population and Reproductive Health, USA), Sara Seims (The David and Lucile Packard Foundation, UK), Saroj Kumar Sikdar (Ministry of Health, India), Sivanthi Thanenthiran (The Asian-Pacific Resource & Research Centre for Women, Malaysia), Mountaga Toure (The Malian Association for the Protection and Promotion of the Family, Mali), Esther Vicente (University of Puerto Rico, Puerto Rico), and Senorina Wendoh (International Planned Parenthood Federation, UK). Annex C provides summaries and evidence tables based on the GRADE methodology. For example, recommendations on non-discrimination are grounded in human rights standards, with no health evidence sought. Studies on the integration of supply chains and family planning services highlight challenges such as high risk of bias due to differences in baseline and follow-up assessments, small sample sizes, and limited statistical significance between full and partial intervention packages. Comprehensive sexuality education programs, as reviewed by P. Whyte, suggest that theory-based, multi-component educational interventions in high school students face challenges such as self-reported outcome biases, lack of follow-up data, and exploratory rather than confirmatory analyses. Condom use during last intercourse was a secondary outcome, while primary outcomes included frequency of unprotected intercourse and the number of sexual partners without condom use. Curriculum-based programs grounded in social cognitive and inoculation theories for students in grades 6 to 9 also faced high risks of bias due to self-reported surveys, lack of participation, and significant loss to follow-up. Peer-led versus teacher-led sex education programs showed some risk of bias, with outcomes primarily self-reported and limited data on total sample sizes. Studies on the removal of financial barriers to contraceptive access, such as providing methods at no cost, report observational data with serious limitations, including lack of comparison with cost-based contraceptive use and incomplete details on assessed participants. For instance, 67% of women in one study chose long-acting contraceptive methods, but no data on the number assessed were provided. Efforts to improve access to family planning services for rural populations, such as through lady health workers or traditional medical practitioners, face challenges like high bias risks due to observational study designs, lack of baseline data, and limited causal linkages. Community-based approaches in emergency settings, such as refugee populations, also show very low-quality evidence, with significant limitations in data collection and analysis. Integration of family planning with HIV services, as reviewed by Lindgren et al., indicates positive results in increasing contraceptive use, but the evidence is limited to lowand middle-income countries, with no pooled analyses provided. Similarly, postpartum contraceptive counseling interventions show mixed results, with high risks of selection and reporting biases. Overall, the evidence presented in these annexes highlights the complexities and limitations of current research in family planning and reproductive health interventions, emphasizing the need for rigorous study designs and comprehensive data collection to inform policy and practice.
